content: 1. Individuals and families should be actively involved in their own healthcare by making informed decisions. This approach encourages personal engagement and support in managing their health. 2. People should be encouraged to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) as soon as possible, including the option for same-day initiation, provided there are no clinical contraindications. 3. HIV testing services (HTS) should be routinely offered to all key populations in both community and facility-based settings. Dual HIV/syphilis testing is recommended for key populations. 4. Community-based HIV testing, linked to prevention, treatment, and care, should be made available in addition to routine facility-based testing for key populations in all settings. This is strongly recommended despite low-certainty evidence. 5. Adolescents from key populations should have access to HIV testing services linked to prevention, treatment, and care. They should also receive counseling on the benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV-positive status and be supported in deciding if, when, how, and to whom to disclose. 6. In high HIV burden settings, HTS linked to prevention, treatment, and care is recommended for all adolescents. In low HIV burden settings, these services should be accessible to adolescents, particularly those from key populations. 7. For children and adolescents who have been sexually abused, WHO recommends offering HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), emergency contraception (for pre-pubertal girls), and presumptive treatment or syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in settings where laboratory testing is not feasible. 8. Adolescent girls aged 9–14 years should be offered human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination according to national guidelines. 9. Governments should revisit age-of-consent policies to uphold adolescents' rights to make decisions about their health and well-being, considering their maturity and understanding. 10. All pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once, ideally during their first antenatal care visit. In high HIV burden settings or among key populations, pregnant women should be retested in the third trimester or during labor and delivery. 11. HIV-exposed infants should undergo virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age or as soon as possible thereafter. Point-of-care nucleic acid testing is recommended for diagnosing HIV in infants and children under 18 months of age. 12. Infants with an initial positive virological test result should start ART immediately while awaiting confirmatory test results. Immediate ART initiation saves lives and should not be delayed. 13. Rapid diagnostic tests for HIV serology can be used to assess HIV exposure in infants younger than four months. For infants and children aged 4–18 months, HIV exposure status should be determined by testing the mother. 14. Children aged 18 months or older with suspected HIV infection or exposure should undergo HIV serological testing according to the standard diagnostic algorithm used for adults. 15. In high HIV burden settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics should be routinely tested for HIV. 16. Network-based testing, including testing biological children of people with HIV and within social networks, is recommended. Family and household testing services and partner services are also strongly recommended. 17. National regulatory agencies are encouraged to adopt point-of-care early infant diagnosis (EID) through streamlined registration and approval processes to enable immediate implementation. 18. Couples and partners of people with HIV, as well as those at ongoing risk, should be offered network-based testing, including social network testing, family and household testing services, and partner services. 19. STI partner services should be offered to individuals with STIs as part of a comprehensive package of voluntary STI testing, care, and prevention. These services must always be voluntary, never mandatory, and ensure privacy and confidentiality. 20. Women who disclose intimate partner violence or sexual assault should be offered immediate support, including first-line support from healthcare providers or accessible alternatives. 21. Healthcare providers should inquire about exposure to intimate partner violence when assessing conditions potentially caused or complicated by such violence to improve diagnosis and care. 22. HIV testing services aim to deliver accurate diagnoses promptly and facilitate access to prevention, treatment, and care, including ART, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and other interventions. 23. Despite significant progress in scaling up HIV testing services globally, gaps remain, particularly among key populations, adult men, partners of people living with HIV, adolescents, and children. 24. Countries should use data to refine their HIV response by identifying patterns of transmission in specific groups or locations to focus prevention strategies where they will have the greatest impact. 25. Integration of HIV testing services into other health services is increasingly important, as it is cost-effective and provides client-centered care. Tools like dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests and self-tests offer unique opportunities for integration. 26. Linkage to prevention, treatment, and care following HIV testing is essential for programmatic impact. Immediate ART initiation and improved treatment options have increased access and uptake of treatment. 27. Efforts should focus on preventing misdiagnosis of HIV status by ensuring the use of optimal testing algorithms and up-to-date strategies, particularly in resource-limited settings. 28. Despite increased access to HIV testing services, many individuals at the highest risk of HIV remain untested and unreached. Priority populations include those most affected by HIV, critical to achieving low incidence, or with specific vulnerabilities. 29. Countries should support the integration of HIV testing services into broader health services, including TB, STIs, viral hepatitis, and non-communicable diseases, to provide effective, client-centered care.
